chapter.name: Timeline and Sources of History
chapter.blurb: History is the study of the human past, studied not just by historians but also by geologists, palaeontologists, anthropologists and archaeologists. Time is measured using the Gregorian calendar's CE (Common Era) and BCE (Before Common Era) system; because there is no year zero, calculating years between a BCE and a CE date means adding the two numbers and subtracting one. Timelines, centuries (100 years) and millenniums (1,000 years) help order events. A source of history -- archaeological, oral, literary or artistic -- is any place, person, text or object that tells us about the past, though gaps often remain. Modern humans have existed for about 300,000 years, beginning as hunter-gatherer bands before settling into farming villages and, eventually, towns, aided by new technologies like pottery and metal.

scope_in.item: History is the study of the human past; the four specialists named as studying it are geologists (the Earth's physical features), palaeontologists (fossil remains of plants, animals and humans), anthropologists (human societies and cultures) and archaeologists (excavated remains such as tools, pots, beads and bones); other contributors include historians, epigraphists (ancient inscriptions), experts in literature and languages, and, in the last 50 years, scientific studies (climate, chemistry, genetics); for recent history, newspapers and electronic media are also consulted

The Gregorian calendar (12 months, 365 days, a leap year every four years, except that century years are leap years only if they are a multiple of 400, so only 2000 among 1800/1900/2000) is used worldwide alongside calendars such as Hindu, Muslim, Jewish and Chinese; years are labelled CE (Common Era, formerly AD) after the conventional starting point and BCE (Before Common Era, formerly BC) before it, e.g. 1947 CE, 560 BCE

There is no year zero: year 1 CE follows immediately after year 1 BCE; the number of years between a BCE date and a CE date is found by adding the two year numbers and subtracting 1 (e.g. 2 BCE to 2 CE = 2+2-1 = 3 years; the Buddha, born 560 BCE, was born 560+2024-1 = 2,583 years before 2024 CE)

A timeline shows a sequence of dates and events and helps establish their order; a century is a period of 100 years counted from year 1 CE (the 21st century CE = 2001-2100), and centuries BCE are counted backward from 1 BCE (the 3rd century BCE = 300-201 BCE); a millennium is a period of 1,000 years (the 3rd millennium CE = 2001-3000 CE), and millenniums BCE are likewise counted backward from 1 BCE (the 1st millennium BCE = 1-1000 BCE); a decade is a period of 10 years

A source of history is a place, person, text or object providing information about a past event or period; sources may be incomplete, or may confirm or contradict each other, requiring historians to judge which to trust; Archaeological Sources include Inscriptions (manuscripts, copper plates, coins), Structures (monuments, mounds) and Excavations (human/animal/plant remains, tools and weapons, figurines and ornaments, pottery and toys, habitations and burials); Oral Sources include genealogical accounts and folklore; Artistic Sources include paintings, sculptures and panels

Literary Sources are divided into Indian Literature (Vedas and Itihasas, poems and plays, historical texts, collection of stories, scientific and technological texts) and Foreign Accounts (travelogues, historical chronicles)

Modern humans (Homo sapiens) have lived on Earth for about 300,000 years; early humans lived in bands in temporary camps, rock shelters or caves, were hunter-gatherers, used fire, made stone tools (axes, blades, arrowheads), created rock art, and made ornaments (stone or shell beads, animal-teeth pendants) which they exchanged with other groups; the last Ice Age lasted from roughly 100,000 years ago to around 12,000 years ago

After the Ice Age, communities settled, often near rivers for water and fertile soil, cultivated cereals and grains, and domesticated animals such as cattle and goats; social complexity grew, with chieftains responsible for community well-being, collective (not individual) land ownership, hamlets growing into villages that exchanged goods, and networks between villages, some of which grew into small towns; new technologies (pottery, then copper and later iron metallurgy) produced more durable tools, objects and ornaments

concepts.name: History and how we study the past
concepts.description: History is the study of the human past; various specialists -- geologists, palaeontologists, anthropologists, archaeologists, historians and others -- each contribute differently to reconstructing it.
concepts.idea: History is the study of the human past, and many different kinds of specialists contribute to understanding it, not historians alone.
concepts.rule: Geologists study the Earth's physical features; palaeontologists study fossil remains of plants, animals and humans; anthropologists study human societies and cultures; archaeologists dig up and study remains people left behind, such as tools, pots and bones.
concepts.example: An archaeologist digging up ancient pots and beads, and a palaeontologist studying a fossilised footprint, are both helping piece together the human past, but through different kinds of evidence.

concepts.name: Measuring time: the Gregorian calendar and CE/BCE terminology
concepts.description: The Gregorian calendar is the world's most common calendar; years are labelled CE (Common Era, formerly AD) or BCE (Before Common Era, formerly BC), counted forward or backward from a conventional starting point.
concepts.idea: Different societies have their own ways of measuring time, but the Gregorian calendar is now used worldwide alongside other calendars like Hindu, Muslim, Jewish and Chinese.
concepts.rule: Years after the conventional birth of Jesus are marked CE (Common Era, earlier AD); years before it are marked BCE (Before Common Era, earlier BC); for example, 1947 CE is the year India became independent.
concepts.example: 560 BCE, the approximate year of the Buddha's birth, is written using BCE because it falls before the conventional starting point of the calendar.

concepts.name: Calculating years: the no-year-zero rule and years-between formula
concepts.description: Because the Gregorian calendar has no year zero, the number of years between a BCE date and a CE date is found by adding the two numbers and subtracting one.
concepts.idea: There is no 'year zero' in the Gregorian calendar -- the year 1 CE follows immediately after the year 1 BCE.
concepts.rule: To calculate the number of years between a BCE date and a CE date, add the two year numbers and subtract 1, e.g. 2 BCE to 2 CE is 2 + 2 - 1 = 3 years.
concepts.example: If the Buddha was born in 560 BCE and the current year is taken as 2024 CE, then the Buddha was born 560 + 2024 - 1 = 2,583 years ago.

concepts.name: Timelines, centuries and millenniums
concepts.description: A timeline shows a sequence of dates and events; a century is a 100-year period and a millennium a 1,000-year period, both counted from year 1 CE forward and year 1 BCE backward.
concepts.idea: A timeline is a tool that shows a sequence of dates and events, helping us see the order in which things happened even without remembering exact dates.
concepts.rule: A century is any period of 100 years, counted from year 1 CE (the 21st century CE runs 2001-2100); a millennium is any period of 1,000 years (the 3rd millennium CE runs 2001-3000 CE); BCE centuries and millenniums are counted backward from 1 BCE.
concepts.example: The 3rd century BCE covers the years 300 BCE to 201 BCE, and the 1st millennium BCE covers 1 BCE to 1000 BCE.

concepts.name: Sources of history: Archaeological, Oral and Artistic sources
concepts.description: A source of history is any place, person, text or object providing information about the past; archaeological sources include inscriptions, structures and excavated finds, oral sources include genealogies and folklore, and artistic sources include paintings, sculptures and panels.
concepts.idea: A source of history is a place, person, text or object from which we gather information about a past event or period.
concepts.rule: Archaeological sources include inscriptions (manuscripts, copper plates, coins), structures (monuments, mounds) and excavations (remains, tools and weapons, figurines and ornaments, pottery and toys, habitations and burials); oral sources include genealogical accounts and folklore; artistic sources include paintings, sculptures and panels.
concepts.example: An old coin dug up at an excavation site is an archaeological source (an inscription), while a grandmother's story passed down through a family is an oral source.

questions.q: Explain why the chapter warns that 'quite a few pieces of the puzzle may remain missing' when studying history through its sources.

concepts.name: Sources of history: Literary sources -- Indian Literature and Foreign Accounts
concepts.description: Literary sources of history split into Indian Literature (Vedas and Itihasas, poems and plays, historical texts, collections of stories, scientific and technological texts) and Foreign Accounts (travelogues and historical chronicles written by outside visitors).
concepts.idea: Literary sources of history come both from within a land, as Indian Literature, and from outside visitors, as Foreign Accounts.
concepts.rule: Indian Literature as a source includes the Vedas and Itihasas, poems and plays, historical texts, collections of stories, and scientific and technological texts; Foreign Accounts include travelogues and historical chronicles written by foreign travellers or writers.
concepts.example: A foreign traveller's written account of their journey through ancient India is a travelogue, a type of Foreign Account, while the Vedas are part of India's own literary tradition.

concepts.name: Early humans and the growth of communities
concepts.description: Early Homo sapiens lived as hunter-gatherer bands using fire, tools, rock art and ornaments; after the Ice Age, communities settled near rivers, took up farming, and grew into villages and towns using new technologies like pottery and metal.
concepts.idea: Modern humans have lived on Earth for about 300,000 years, first as hunter-gatherer bands, and later as settled farming communities that grew more socially complex over time.
concepts.rule: Early humans lived in bands in temporary camps, rock shelters or caves, used fire and stone tools, made rock art and ornaments; after the last Ice Age (roughly 100,000 to 12,000 years ago) ended, many communities settled near rivers, cultivated crops, domesticated animals, and grew into villages and towns using pottery and metal (copper, then iron).
concepts.example: A community that once hunted and gathered its food eventually settled beside a river, grew crops, and later exchanged pottery and metal tools with neighbouring villages as it grew into a small town.
